title: AutoSecAudit: An Extensible Multi-Scanner Orchestration Framework with AI-Assisted Remediation Guidance, Precision Fuzzing, and Delta Auditing in DevSecOps
abstract: Automating security verification in fast-paced continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines creates operational friction: studies of developer tool adoption report that noisy output and missing actionable guidance discourage the use of automated analysis tools [13].This paper presents AutoSecAudit, an open, extensible dynamic application security testing (DAST) orchestration framework with remediation guidance, designed for CI/CD pipelines and AI developer tooling.It combines (1) attack-surface discovery through a depth-limited recursive crawler, JavaScript route extraction, OpenAPI import, and a scope guard that checks every resolved address; (2) concurrent execution of 19 scanner plugins with heuristic false-positive reduction (baseline-response comparison, a two-phase statistical timing check, single-page-application filtering, and adaptive politeness with retry on HTTP 429/503); (3) an intelligence layer that merges duplicate findings on a canonical key, enriches CVE-tagged findings with CVSS data, maps findings to OWASP Top 10 (2021), CWE, and PCI DSS v4.0 by keyword rules, and assigns plain-English businessrisk categories and a five-level posture grade; and (4) delivery features: predefined multi-framework fix recipes, fingerprint-based delta comparison between scans, severity gating through exit codes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with four tools for AI coding assistants.Applying patches is left to the assistant or developer, and closedloop remediation is not evaluated.We evaluate the tool on two purpose-built test applications with 17 and 8 planted vulnerabilities, using 5 repetitions per setting on one Windows machine.Testbed 2 was fully detected with no false positive in all 5 runs, whereas testbed 1 was fully detected in 3 of 5 runs (mean recall 81%) because some scans reached the 300 s scan deadline.None of these measured runs reported a false positive, but one further testbed 2 run inside the test suite did (a missing-SameSite cookie finding that matched no planted item).Merging reduced raw plugin alerts by 21% and 22% on complete scans.Increasing worker threads from 1 to 16 did not shorten scans (median 53 s at k=1 and 53 s at k=16), so an earlier speedup claim is withdrawn, and 10 of 25 scans ran longer than the 56 s floor.Delta comparison was exact on two complete scans but produced spurious changes when scans were incomplete.These results come from one machine and small applications written alongside the tool; they say nothing about performance on production applications.
authors: Kodi Vishruth Aithal; Thilak N; Vinaya Kumar B; Vishal Gowda B; Ranjitha R

title: ON-PREMISE OPEN-WEIGHT LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR INTERPRETABLE WEB VULNERABILITY DETECTION: A BENCHMARK AGAINST CLOUD MODELS AND RULE-BASED STATIC ANALYSIS
abstract: Organisations handling regulated or proprietary source code are frequently prohibited from transmitting it to third-party inference providers, which excludes commercial cloud large language models from their security-analysis pipelines regardless of the accuracy those models achieve. Whether self-hosted open-weight models can substitute for them on ordinary developer hardware has not been established. This study benchmarks five quantised open-weight models, from 1.5 to 8 billion parameters and executed entirely on a consumer laptop graphics processor with eight gigabytes of video memory, on 120 annotated web-application code snippets spanning five weakness categories. Each was evaluated under zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and compared against a rule-based static analyser and previously published cloud-model results on the identical corpus. The strongest local configuration reached an F1-score of 0.900, exceeding the previous-generation cloud flagship and trailing the current one by 4.7 points, while generating a remediation suggestion for every correct detection. The analysis further shows that F1 alone conceals degenerate behaviour: several configurations, including one cloud model, approach the score of a classifier labelling every input as vulnerable, so reporting specificity alongside F1 is proposed as a minimum requirement. Privacy-preserving on-premise vulnerability analysis is thus attainable without specialised infrastructure.
authors: Ilya Andreevich Shelestov

title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling
abstract: Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository. The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.
authors: Rui Melo; André Duarte; Aditya Oke; Shubham Gandhi; Nachiket Kotalwar; Rui Abreu; Lei Li; Carolyn Rose

title: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) reports flag operations whose safety depends on project-specific context, and maintainers must decide which reports describe real defects. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret this context, but adjudicating a report with them requires the decisive code, which often lies far from the reported line, and a decision basis that program analysis can check. We present VulnSAGE, an adjudication system for SAST reports that connects LLM reasoning to program structure in both directions. Its report-centered slicer recovers the dependencies of the reported operation together with the program structure that explains them, such as the caller object on which a helper acts. CLAIM, an intermediate representation for report judgments, records each model interpretation as a semantic fact that cites the program relations it assumes. Program analysis checks these premises, and the verdict follows from the facts whose premises hold. Both mechanisms share a program graph, which lets the model cite the code it reads and lets the checker query those citations. Statically supported true positives then guide proof-of-concept generation and runtime reproduction. Across 187 labeled reports from four corpora covering five vulnerability families, VulnSAGE rejects 89 of 97 false alarms and retains 85 of 90 real defects. Under a common PoC procedure, 25 of its positive verdicts reproduce at runtime, compared with three for the LLM-based adjudicator LLM4SA. Applied to 45,440 alerts raised by five SAST tools on the 200 most-starred C/C++ projects on GitHub, it reproduces 104 defects at runtime. Maintainers have confirmed 24 of the 26 defects they have responded to, including ten previously unknown defects, nine of which are already fixed.
authors: Jin-Bao Chen; Zi-Xiang Zhou; Yu Zhang; Yi-Hong Wu

title: Agentic and generative AI for intelligent autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing: A systematic analysis
abstract: Context: Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) is increasingly challenged by the scale, heterogeneity, and dynamic nature of modern digital infrastructures, particularly across enterprise IT, operational technology (OT), industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and cyber–physical systems. Although Agentic AI and Generative AI have each shown promise for automating parts of security auditing, the current literature remains fragmented across isolated audit phases and is still dominated by conventional IT-centric perspectives. Objectives: This paper systematically analyses recent advances in Agentic AI, Reinforcement Learning (RL), Large Language Models (LLMs), and tool-augmented Generative AI for autonomous VAPT. It aims to synthesise how these paradigms support end-to-end security auditing, identify the principal technical, operational, and governance gaps in the literature, and derive an evidence-grounded reference model for trustworthy autonomous auditing across both IT and OT environments. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted across major scholarly databases, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. From 1144 initially identified records, 72 studies were retained after deduplication, screening, and full-text eligibility assessment. Included studies were coded across five attributes and synthesised into thematic trajectories to derive the proposed framework. Study credibility was screened against three qualitative, non-instrumented criteria—venue and editorial process, presence of empirical or systematic conceptual evaluation, and explicit acknowledgement of limitations. Results: The review shows that agentic approaches are best suited to sequential and adaptive tasks such as reconnaissance orchestration, exploit-path selection, lateral movement, post-exploitation pivoting, and adaptive re-testing. In contrast, generative approaches are strongest in reasoning over unstructured evidence, interpreting configurations and advisories, contextualising vulnerabilities, assessing exploit feasibility, mapping compliance controls, and producing traceable audit reports. However, few studies integrate these capabilities into a governed end-to-end workflow, and real-world OT/Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) validation remains limited. Of the 72 coded studies, 56 apply classical machine or deep learning, 14 use generative/LLM techniques, and only 2 employ reinforcement-learning or agentic control; none is evaluated against a physical or emulated OT/IIoT target, and reported autonomy is strongly scaffolding-dependent (for example, 21% fully autonomous versus 64% human-assisted task completion on AutoPenBench, an external benchmark outside the coded corpus). To address these gaps, this paper derives a unified Agentic–Generative VAPT model comprising four tightly coupled layers: agentic decision-making, generative reasoning, structured tool interfaces, and validation–governance. It further introduces a formal threat and evaluation abstraction for Model Context Protocol (MCP)-style interface layers and proposes a five-dimensional VAPT Autonomy Benchmark for future empirical validation. Conclusion: Autonomous security auditing is evolving from isolated AI-assisted tasks towards integrated, policy-constrained, and auditable architectures. Nevertheless, major challenges remain in hallucination control, prompt injection, sparse reward design, explainability, safety-aware evaluation, and benchmark standardisation. Future research should prioritise tightly integrated agentic–generative systems, realistic and safety-aware IT/OT testbeds, and governance mechanisms that enable trustworthy human-in-the-loop deployment in operational environments.
authors: Samuel Roy Anthony Truss; Mohamed Chahine Ghanem; Mohammed Amin Almaiah; Marco Ortolani; Mohammed B. M. Kamel; Tayeb Kenaza; Tatiana Kalganova

title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
abstract: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.
authors: Michele Guerra; Wuyeh Jobe; Sanjana Nambiar; Christina Pöpper; Azza Abouzied

title: From Code Author to Code Reviewer: A Systematic Review of Practitioner Experience with Generative AI in Software Engineering
abstract: Practitioner use of generative AI in software engineering has progressed faster than the evidence assessing its effects. This review examined 58 empirical studies published from 2024 to early 2026 on GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Using PRISMA-guided selection from five digital libraries, the studies addressed productivity, role shifts, code quality, adoption behaviour, and evidence gaps. Findings were synthesised into the AI Integration Consequence Model, a conceptual four-layer framework linking adoption conditions, role shifts, quality exposure, and organisational consequences. Evidence indicates that developers increasingly move from code production to code review, as more than half of AI-generated code is discarded after evaluation. Generative AI improves efficiency for boilerplate code, documentation, and unit-test scaffolding, but provides limited benefits for architectural decisions and enterprise debugging. A meta-analysis of 47 studies reported a 45.6-point gap between self-reported and objectively measured productivity. AI-generated code also showed exploitable vulnerabilities at estimated rates of 40–50%, varying by task, tool version, programming language, and measurement method. Social influence strongly predicted adoption intent, while concerns about peer judgement encouraged undisclosed use. Experienced engineers generally received an AI Boost, whereas junior engineers faced an AI Drag. Structured mentorship reduced this gap in one 14-month cohort study. Key evidence gaps include cross-cultural adoption, longitudinal skill development, and unreplicated gender disparities.
authors: Bassey Echeng Isong; Tshipuke Vahangwele; Nosipho Dladlu
venue: Journal of Information Systems and Informatics

title: From Prose to Properties: Testing Research Claims with ARATest for Agent-Native Science
abstract: AI agents now run experiments and report findings, so research produces claims faster than researchers can check them. Each empirical claim implies a property that must hold over its cases, but it states that property only in prose. Without an explicit property, no test can decide which evidence would falsify a claim, so validation cannot keep pace with the claims agents produce. To make claims testable, we approximate a claim's semantics by abstracting its property skeleton, a parameterized relation that recurs across claims. We present ARATest, a property-based testing library that checks these skeletons as executable tests. A typed declaration binds a claim to a skeleton and fixes the claim's compared quantities, cases, scope, and numerical policy. A shared case type makes every generator supply cases in the claim's statistical unit. A three-valued semantics assigns each property one of three verdicts: holds, violated, or inconclusive. Every violation carries a replayable witness. A default generator reads the evidence that agent-native research artifacts (ARA) link to each claim, and auto-research generators dispatch an agent to run released code for fresh cases. Our DissClaimer plugin supplies that agent and runs these generators as continuous testing. Of 243 claims in 33 ARA artifacts, 54 received faithful declarations bound to evidence: 32 held, eight were violated, and 14 remained inconclusive. Two violations exposed errors in published papers that their authors confirmed. ARATest detected all 553 seeded faults without a false alarm on 19 valid controls, outperforming two LLM judges. Fresh runs exposed behaviors that reported evidence could not show. These results suggest that one fixed test can check explicit claim properties against both reported and fresh evidence.
authors: Yifeng He; Jiachen Liu; Hao Chen

title: How Much Does the Harness Matter, and for Whom? A Multi-Model Study of Context in LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery
abstract: How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.
authors: Ganni Galea Curmi; Ben Wilde

title: Secure Agentic Coding through Counterexample-Grounded Feedback
abstract: As coding models and agent harnesses become more capable, reliable security verification is becoming a central bottleneck. Improving secure code generation requires a signal whose reported progress remains aligned with actual program behavior under optimization; otherwise, an optimizer can improve the signal's verdict without removing the underlying vulnerability. Existing model-based approaches require models to either infer program behavior from source code or specify correct outcomes for adversarial tests, placing substantial reasoning demands on the security signal. We introduce \falcon{}, a counterexample-grounded verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification and connects them through execution traces of the program under test. In test-time repair, \falcon{} yields substantially stronger held-out functional-security gains than alternative security signals across secure code generation benchmarks, while preserving or improving functionality. As an RL reward, \falcon{} also outperforms static-analysis and learned rewards on held-out functional-security, even when all policies successfully optimize their respective training rewards. Combining \falcon{} with either proxy reward further improves held-out performance, suggesting that execution-grounded feedback can mitigate reward overoptimization while preserving useful guidance from existing security signals.
authors: Tue Le; Anh Nguyen Hoang; Gabriel Sasseville; Doseok Jang; Pierre‐Luc Bacon; Nghi D. Q. Bui

title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
abstract: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. On 63,684 programs generated by 12 models for 899 tasks, SPLASH picks secure code in 74% of cases, places the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs, and chooses better than a frontier LLM judge.
authors: Mirza Masfiqur Rahman; Ajwad Akil; Imtiaz Karim; Ashish Kundu; Ramana Rao Kompella; Elisa Bertino

title: AgenticVulHunter: Bringing Local Agentic Vulnerability Hunting to Your Terminal
abstract: Finding vulnerabilities early, before they can affect the production system, is important for reducing the risk of any software attacks. However, detecting vulnerabilities during secure code review is still difficult because the vulnerable code logic may depend on lines found across different repository files. Recent approaches such as AgenticSCR have shown that LLM agents can explore repository files and use security knowledge to improve secure code review. However, these approaches mainly rely on external commercial LLMs and can provide a large amount of security knowledge to the agent at once. This creates an important question of whether agentic secure code review can also be performed effectively using locally deployed open-weight LLMs with more focused and relevant security knowledge. In this paper, we propose AgenticVulHunter, an agentic secure code review approach and tool that can run with a locally deployed open-weight LLM. We evaluate AgenticVulHunter on 144 vulnerability cases from SCRBench using Qwen3-Coder-30B and DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus. We measure what percentage of generated review comments correctly identify the vulnerable location, match the vulnerability type, and provide a relevant security review comment together. AgenticVulHunter achieves an accuracy of 18.4% with Qwen3- Coder-30B and 23.8% with DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus, compared with 11.8% for our AgenticSCR-style reproduction using Qwen3-Coder-30B and 17.5% for AgenticSCR using Claude Sonnet 4.
authors: Nishant Abhishek; Ping Charoenwet; Kla Tantithamthavorn

title: A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and Compliance Implications
abstract: Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation
authors: David Excel Ozowara
venue: Science Education and Innovations in the Context of Modern Problems

title: Cyber Defence, Agentic AI, and the Sociotechnical Paradigm: A Survey of AI-Driven Cybersecurity
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.
authors: Rupsingh Puransingh Mathwale
venue: International Journal of Applied Smart Interdisciplinary Technologies

title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack
abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.
authors: Justin Tan; Miao Li; Ding Zhao

title: mzCache: On-Device LLM Memory Management under Multitasking
abstract: On-device mobile Large Language Model (LLM) inference is gaining significant attention. However, mobile devices operate in highly dynamic multitasking environments where users frequently switch between applications. This creates memory pressure, forcing LLM memory—model weights and KV cache—to be evicted by the operating system. When a new inference request arrives, the inference system must restore the evicted memory through slow storage reads or recompute the entire KV cache, severely degrading responsiveness. To address this, we present mzCache, an on-device LLM inference system with specialized memory management for multitasking environments. Under unpredictable memory pressure, mzCache elastically evicts LLM memory and leverages the unified memory of mobile SoCs to enable zero-wait inference on the GPU with concurrent CPU-side restoration. mzCache realizes this through restoration-oriented memory management: LLM memory is partitioned into fine-grained shared buffers to enable partial eviction and restoration with concurrent cross-processor access, while hybrid swap and backward-out eviction policies ensure low-latency restoration from any eviction state. Implemented on llama.cpp and deployed as an Android application, mzCache achieves 2.1–5.5× reduction in Time-to-First-Token compared to storage-backed partial offload and demonstrates its effectiveness in real multitasking scenarios.
authors: Hongseung Yu; Minsung Kim; Jongseok Park; Kyunghan Lee
venue: ACM Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom)

title: AI-Assisted DevSecOps for Secure Software Delivery in Earth Observation Projects
abstract: As the Cloud Systems Team at ECMWF, we operate and secure the distributed cloud infrastructures — Kubernetes clusters hosted on OpenStack-based private clouds, including the EWC (European Weather Cloud, co-managed by ECMWF and EUMETSAT) and partner sites — that underpin EU-funded Earth Observation platforms in the scope of this paper. In this environment, container images may accumulate CVEs silently between builds, manual remediation backlogs can grow faster than our team can clear, and static analysis alone cannot generally distinguish exploitable from theoretical vulnerabilities. We present the AI Software Security Agent, a fully automated, Large Language Model (LLM)-powered platform that integrates into existing CI/CD pipelines to perform four complementary security tasks without human intervention: (i) container image hardening through iterative scanning and LLM-driven patching, eliminating CRITICAL and HIGH CVEs; (ii) source code remediation of BLOCKER and CRITICAL issues via targeted LLM-generated fixes validated by the existing test suite; (iii) automated unit test enhancement using coverage-driven LLM prompts that increased test coverage by up to 39 percentage points; and (iv) automated penetration testing to classify each CVE by real-world exploitability. The system is orchestrated at the CI/CD level, and all LLM inference runs on-premise via Ollama on dedicated GPU nodes, ensuring that source code and vulnerability data never leave the organisation’s perimeter. A YAML-driven configuration system provides multi-language support for .NET/C#, Python, Java, and Node.js which can be easily extended to other languages. We describe the architecture, the iterative fix-and-verify methodology, and results from deployment on four real-world Earth Observation applications.
authors: F. Fornari; Mohanad Albughdadi; Marica Antonacci; Vasileios Baousis; Tolga Kaprol; Claudio Pisa

title: SentinelML: Behavioral Machine-Learning-Based Ransomware Detection with Decoupled AI Security Analysis
abstract: Ransomware remains a critical threat to modern enterprise and personal computing infrastructure.Traditional signature-based detection mechanisms exhibit operational degradation when confronted with previously unobserved polymorphic or zero-day variants.This paper presents SentinelML, an autonomous endpoint detection architecture that identifies ransomware activity through 19 dynamic behavioral indicators collected entirely in user space without requiring kernel-level filter drivers.By sampling filesystem Shannon entropy, process concurrency anomalies, shadow copy deletion commands, and cryptographic module bindings, SentinelML trains a local Random Forest classifier that operates as an unprivileged host daemon.To address operational triage transparency, the local classifier is coupled with an architecturally decoupled Large Language Model (LLM) advisory explainer operating via an isolated HTTPS interface.We conduct an exhaustive technical audit of the production system: confirming that Shannon entropy accounts for 41.31% of aggregate Gini importance, documenting the operational tradeoffs of heuristic user-space proxies, analyzing platform asymmetry between Windows and Linux deployments, and evaluating the system strictly as an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).Finally, we disclose that previously reported internal metrics (0.9567 accuracy across candidate algorithms) could not be independently reproduced due to unpreserved training artifacts, and establish an open empirical evaluation protocol for reproducible validation.
authors: Vasu Chowdary; Moulica Chowdary; D. M. Yashaswini; Rajashree M. Byalal

title: Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability."
authors: Gadi Evron

title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
authors: Han Zhou; Yu Luo; Dianxiang Xu

title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond
abstract: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, among the crashes discovered by 5uGUE, MediaTek has confirmed two new high-severity vulnerabilities, with one CVE assigned (CVE-2026-20525), while UNISOC confirmed seven crashes. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our evaluations, 5uGUE finds an average of 6.4 novel crashes and 1.6 unique crashes. In a nutshell, 5uGUE highlights that LLM agents are capable to operate effectively beyond software-in-the-loop settings, extending autonomous vulnerability discovery to the proprietary, hardware-bound systems that affect billions of end-user devices across multiple wireless protocols.
authors: Guoqiang Hua; Udeshi Sakshi; Matheus Eduardo Garbelini; Daisuke Mashima; Sudipta Chattopadhyay

title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
abstract: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities. We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives. Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach. The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks. In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models. Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%. Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy. These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.
authors: Yiheng Li; Jingyue Li

title: Raise or Check? Predicting the Necessity of Additional Fuzzing for Continuous Fuzzing
abstract: Continuous fuzzing is used for vulnerability detection in Open Source Software (OSS). Large-scale services such as Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzz over 1,300 projects and have revealed more than 10,000 vulnerabilities. Despite this, a considerable time lag often exists between when a vulnerability is introduced and when it is detected (i.e., the window of exposure). Given the computational cost of additional fuzzing, we aim to allocate fuzzing resources efficiently using vulnerability-risk estimates. We propose RAISE (Risk-Aware Intensive Supplemental Execution Framework), a Just-In-Time (JIT) framework that prioritizes additional fuzzing for high-risk project-days. RAISE performs binary classification at the project-day granularity to estimate whether a vulnerability is introduced on a given day. We construct a dataset combining vulnerability-introducing commits from the OSV database with daily coverage and change metrics from OSS-Fuzz, covering 15 C/C++ projects and 15,210 project-days, of which 347 (2.28%) are vulnerability-introducing. In a cross-project validation setting, our best model, a Random Forest combining VCCFinder-based static features with dynamic fuzzing features, achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.74, substantially outperforming a random baseline; coverage metrics, led by PatchCoverage, are the most important features. In a simulation over 968 vulnerabilities comparing five allocation strategies, Simple-Regression was significantly more cost-efficient than the prediction-agnostic heuristics, spending 91.60 additional fuzzing sessions per detected vulnerability, roughly half the cost of the Median heuristic (171.89). RAISE shows that JIT vulnerability prediction with coverage-aware fuzzing features can effectively guide risk-aware allocation of continuous fuzzing resources.
authors: Riku Kato; Tatsuya Shirai; Olivier Nourry; Yutaro Kashiwa; Kenji Fujiwara; Yasutaka Kamei; Hajimu Iida

title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
abstract: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.
authors: Vita Santa Barletta; Danilo Caivano; Gabriel Cellammare; Andrea Dimauro; Pasquale Mesagna; Massimiliano Morga

title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation
abstract: Code translation converts source code from one programming language to another while preserving its functionality. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved code translation, their outputs still contain hallucinations: generated code that conflicts with the source program, violates target-language facts, or introduces contextually inconsistent dependencies. These failures are especially harmful in translation because small semantic deviations can silently change program behavior. Existing hallucination studies mainly focus on natural-language generation or code generation, leaving the forms, distribution, and mitigation of hallucinations in cross-language code translation insufficiently characterized. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLM hallucinations in code translation. Across three benchmark datasets, six language pairs, and seven LLMs, we construct a taxonomy with three major categories: Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts, and Project Context Deviations. We manually annotate 13,919 hallucination cases and analyze how hallucination types vary across models, datasets, and language directions. Guided by the taxonomy, we further propose HaluCodeTran, a mitigation framework that combines BM25-based retrieval of relevant translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement. The study provides an execution-tested characterization of code-translation hallucinations and a practical baseline for building more reliable LLM-based code migration tools.
authors: Yali Du; Yunji Zhang; Ming Li

title: A Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Engine for Compilation-Free Patch Presence Testing
abstract: Code reuse in modern software ecosystems facilitates the spread of 1-day vulnerabilities, posing significant security risks. Determining if patches are present is crucial, but traditional methods suffer from limited usability and accuracy, often depending on a fragile compilation process. In our prior work, we introduced Lares, the first compilation-free framework for patch presence testing that combines large language models (LLMs) with SMT solvers. However, Lares treats the LLM and the SMT solver as two separate, parallel decision channels: the symbolic channel (Z3) succeeded in only 20% of code cases, and the remaining cases fell back to the neural channel (the LLM) for the final decision. Letting the LLM act as the final arbiter turns verification into an informal, non-deterministic process that is prone to hallucination errors, while the two channels never reinforce each other. To overcome these limitations, we propose SyLares, which reformulates compilation-free patch presence testing as neuro-symbolic reasoning. Instead of letting the LLM emit a final verdict, SyLares uses the LLM as a neural feature extractor that perceives heterogeneous source code and decompiled pseudocode and produces specification-compliant SMT-LIB inputs, and delegates the final, deterministic judgment to the symbolic Z3 solver. This neural-perceives, symbolic-decides coupling is realized by a Code2SMT reasoning engine that combines deterministic syntactic parsing with LLM-driven code normalization and symbol alignment, so that every case is reduced to a formal equivalence query rather than an opaque LLM guess.
authors: Siyuan Li; Jiayi Zhou; Zhiyuan Xia; Weijie Wang; Yaowen Zheng; Weiran Tang; Hong Li; Hongsong Zhu; Shanqing Guo

title: RAGLeak: Supply-Chain Privacy Backdoors in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models to access external knowledge during inference, but its reliance on external knowledge bases also introduces new attack surfaces. Existing data extraction attacks against RAG systems rely on either prompt injection, which heavily depends on the generator's instruction-following capability, or backdoors that reproduce or paraphrase retrieved documents but struggle to balance extraction fidelity and stealthiness. In this paper, we propose RAGLeak, a supply-chain privacy backdoor attack that decouples information leakage from direct textual exposure. When triggered, the generator reversibly obfuscates retrieved private documents for high-fidelity recovery by an auxiliary LLM. Across three model families and three application domains, RAGLeak achieves up to $100\%$ ASR with limited impact on benign utility and at most a $10$-percentage-point ASR drop under representative detection-based defenses. The backdoor remains effective after clean fine-tuning and across model scales and versions, revealing an underexplored supply-chain privacy risk in RAG systems. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGLeak-4B67.
authors: Yuchen Chen; Wei Cheng; Yuan Xiao; Junda He; Jieke Shi; 欧阳萍萍; Quanjun Zhang; Chunrong Fang; David Lo; Zhenyu Chen

title: A Hybrid Information Flow Analysis Framework for Android Hybrid Apps
abstract: The WebView interface in Android (hybrid) applications enables the native side (e.g., Java) to exchange data with the Web (e.g., JavaScript). This creates cross-language information flow channels that existing single-language analyzers cannot analyze. Existing hybrid app analyses address only part of the problem: some build bridge-aware call graphs but provide limited information-flow analysis, some rely on coarse assumptions, and some focus only on web vulnerabilities. We present MifDroid, a static-analysis- guided dynamic-analysis framework with a lifecycle-aware per-WebView call graph, a bridge-aware type-and-effect system, and a modular JavaScript analysis engine. We evaluated MifDroid on 338 apps from the F-Droid repository (out of 4,126 total) that use addJavascriptInterface, enabling active communication between Java and JavaScript. Our guided dynamic phase adds 662 entries to the 444 produced by static analysis, raising the resolution rate from 36.5% to 74.5%, produces the resolved bridge-related entries for 115 apps that static analysis leaves empty. MifDroid reported 14 vulnerable cross-language information flows, five of which have been accepted and fixed by the maintainers.
authors: Jyoti Prakash; Mikkel Baun Kjærgaard; Abhishek Tiwari

title: Global trends and thematic evolution in breast cancer and frailty research: a multi-database bibliometric analysis, 1973–2025
abstract: Background Frailty is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant marker of vulnerability in breast cancer, with implications for treatment tolerance, functional outcomes, and survivorship. This study mapped the global research landscape and thematic evolution of research at the intersection of breast cancer and frailty. Methods Publications were retrieved independently from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), Scopus, and PubMed from database inception through December 31, 2025; publications from 2026 were excluded. After eligibility screening and three-stage cross-database deduplication, 1,003 records were included. Citation analyses were restricted to 591 eligible WoSCC records. Bibliometric analyses were performed using R 4.5.2 with bibliometrix 5.4.0, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace. Results Publication output increased over time and reached 115 records in 2025. Segmented Poisson regression estimated annual rate ratios of 1.133 (95% CI, 1.119–1.147) before 2018 and 1.151 (95% CI, 1.105–1.200) after 2018, but the change in slope was not statistically significant (P = 0.465). The United States ranked first in publication output, the Journal of Geriatric Oncology was the most productive journal, and the University of Toronto was the most productive institution. A title/abstract audit of the 1,003-record dataset identified 421 records (41.97%) mentioning both breast cancer and frailty, 83 (8.28%) mentioning breast cancer only, 361 (35.99%) mentioning frailty only, and 138 (13.76%) mentioning neither term category. Keyword and network analyses identified frailty, geriatric assessment, quality of life, comorbidity, treatment, and survivorship as major themes. Conclusion Breast cancer and frailty research has expanded into an interdisciplinary field spanning oncology, geriatric medicine, supportive care, rehabilitation, and survivorship. The findings should be interpreted in light of the broader indexing contexts represented in the retrieved set.
authors: Silu Xiang; Xu Han; 王小毅

title: Lightweight 8D bitwise hyperchaotic encryption with multi-round SPN for secure medical image cloud storage and retrieval
abstract: Abstract The aim of this research is to develop a highly secure and lightweight hyperchaotic sequence generator for medical image encryption suitable for healthcare cloud systems. Secure transmission of medical images through cloud networks needs strong protection and low computational cost. Most existing hyperchaotic methods use complex multidimensional systems and high resource consumption. These factors reduce their suitability for real-time encryption and cloud-based medical healthcare. They also increase the chances of errors during implementation and raise power requirements. The proposed method uses an 8D bitwise coupled map lattice hyperchaotic sequence generator with a multi-round substitution-permutation network. The system produces eight parallel chaotic sequences with high unpredictability, designed to spread changes across each pixel and bit. The sequence generator uses cross-dimensional feedback and round-based updates to improve key sensitivity and expand the key space. The substitution-permutation network applies repeated nonlinear and spatial transformations using compact S-box and P-box layers. These transformations lower statistical patterns and resist differential analysis. All steps are structured for parallel execution and minimal power use, which is suitable for both cloud and embedded systems. This research evaluates encryption strength and performance using chest X-ray, brain MRI, mammogram, and abdominal CT datasets. The proposed system achieves NPCR of 99.68% and UACI of 33.54% confirming strong differential attack resistance. Key space reaches 2512, derived from the 512-bit SHA-512 key initialization, which exceeds the security threshold of standard 2D, 4D, and 6D chaotic encryption models. Information entropy of encrypted images reaches 7.9997 which is the highest value among all existing methods. Chosen-plaintext attack testing records NPCR of 99.6173% and UACI of 33.4891% meeting the theoretical security threshold. NIST SP 800-22 testing confirms all fifteen randomness tests pass for the discretized 8D keystream. Pixel correlation of encrypted images reaches near zero in all three spatial directions.
authors: Morris C; Devadoss C P; Sujatha V; Beno A

title: Securing Agent-Generated Code with Its Own Development History
abstract: Pull requests written by coding agents can pass a project's test suite while omitting a guard or a validation step. To find the missing condition, a reviewer currently relies on static analysis of the final code. An agent-generated change, however, is accompanied by a development history that a human commit does not provide. The agent's trajectory records each edit together with the agent's stated assumptions, and structural differencing shows how each changed function evolved. We present TRACER, a workflow that uses this development history as evidence for security review. TRACER tracks changes at the symbol level, treats the agent's recorded rationale as claims to be verified against the current code, accepts a repair only after assessment and functional validation, and attaches to each accepted repair an executable check that later changes must satisfy. On the SusVibes benchmark, symbol-level tracking places the vulnerable symbol in the review scope for 94.6% of agent patches, compared with 13.4% for the primary scanner warning. With two investigator models, the configuration that includes the agent's rationale yields the largest number of verified security repairs while preserving functionality, and adding AST history to it does not increase that number. A funnel analysis identifies where the remaining candidates are lost. In a study of structural-biology software, the combination of repair memory and a boundary check allows a subsequent feature request to succeed in nine of ten tasks without reintroducing the repaired vulnerability, whereas functional feedback alone succeeds in four and reintroduces the vulnerability in three.
authors: Prateek Kumar Rajput; Shahzeb Khan; El-Hacen Diallo; Yewei Song; Jacques Klein; Tegawendé F. Bissyandé

title: SemWeaver: Refining LLM-Generated Static Vulnerability Checkers with Analyzer-Internal Evidence
abstract: Recent work shows that LLMs can synthesize static-analysis checkers from security patches, but a compilable checker is not necessarily a correct one. A patch reveals what changed, not why the change is safe, so generated checkers often match only the surface edit and miss the deeper semantic condition. Existing refinement loops feed back compilation errors and validation reports, yet these signals describe symptoms without explaining what the checker misunderstands about the code. We observe that the analysis framework itself already computes the information needed to close this gap. Control-flow graphs, symbolic values, memory regions and checker callbacks are available inside the analyzer but unused by current refinement strategies. SemWeaver is a plug-in refinement layer that extracts patch-relevant analyzer evidence and assembles it with source context and validation feedback into a structured, provenance-labelled bundle. An iterative editing loop refines the checker on both the vulnerable and fixed revisions, guarded by a retention gate that accepts warning recovery or false-positive reduction while preventing over-pruning. We evaluate SemWeaver on 39 KNighter-derived CSA checkers from Linux kernel fixes. With analyzer evidence, refinement reaches 23 warning-positive vulnerable revisions (vs. 15 for KNighter's loop) and raises version-level $F_1$ from 0.448 to 0.575. An ablation removing internal evidence recovers fewer silent cases and produces different checker edits, indicating that the two evidence configurations address complementary recognition gaps. Additional experiments cover three editor models on a 12-subject subset, a CodeQL query refinement, and controlled source-form variations. A qualitative follow-up on all 11 non-tied comparisons traces each warning-count change to a specific checker repair, such as recognizing a lowered callback or unwrapping an expression cast.
authors: Chengzhi Yi; Shenao Wang; Yanjie Zhao; Xiao Cheng; Haoyu Wang

title: From Instructions to Exploits: Applying Program Analysis to Malicious Agent Skills Across Natural Language and Code
abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that combine natural-language instructions with executable code, creating supply-chain risks that may span both artifacts. Existing skill scanners often rely on rule matching or direct LLM judgments and provide limited support for tracing such cross-domain behavior. We present the Supply-Chain Scanner for Agent Skills (SCS), a static analysis framework that unifies instructions and code for security analysis. SCS compiles natural-language instructions into a constrained Python-style intermediate representation using a limited set of security-oriented APIs. It then constructs program dependence graphs for instructions and bundled code and connects them into a cross-domain graph (xPDG). A Trust-Sensitivity-Capability (TSC) model propagates security properties over the graph to support structured, largely deterministic risk detection. On a manually verified benchmark of 117 malicious and 117 benign skills, SCS achieves the highest average accuracy (85.6%), recall (95.2%), and F1-score (86.9%) among evaluated methods across five LLMs, with 80.2% precision and average token consumption of 13.7 million. Its NL-to-IR compiler achieves 92.5%-94.5% step-level correctness on 400 human-annotated instruction steps. Finally, analyzing 66,157 real-world ClawHub skills yields 2,473 candidates, of which 627 are confirmed malicious through auxiliary dynamic validation and manual review.
authors: Shiwu Zhao; Baizhu Wang; Guoqiang Zheng; Tingyu Gao; Yuheng Xie; Rujie Chen; Xingchen Chen; Xuezhang Liu; Qixu Liu

title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
abstract: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.
authors: ZhiHong Liu; Shuyao Gao

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
abstract: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it. We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.
authors: Amine Lbath; Massih-Reza Amini

title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.
authors: Haoran Xue; Nikta Akbarpour; Gias Uddin; Song Wang

title: VulDec: Vulnerability Detection in Binaries via Neural Decompilation
abstract: Automated vulnerability detection in binary executables is challenging due to the lack of source code and the limited semantic information available at the assembly level. Despite significant progress in machine-learning-based code analysis, the field still lacks methodologies and large, high-quality datasets that provide vulnerable code jointly at assembly- and source-level with precise vulnerability labels. To address this gap, we introduce VulDec, consisting of (i) a new large-scale, carefully curated dataset aligning real-world Assembly-C function pairs with detailed CWE annotations across multiple architectures, and (ii) the first end-to-end framework that leverages neural decompilation for binary vulnerability detection. Tuned LLM-based neural decompilers trained on our dataset achieve strong source-level recovery across architectures (Edit Similarity of approximately 56%, BLEU-4 of approximately 43%), while our tuned LLM-based detectors reach a macro F1-score of 0.61 on an in-distribution realistic test set (3% vulnerability rate). Our findings provide evidence that neural decompilation offers a powerful alternative to conventional low-level binary representations, facilitating robust binary vulnerability detection.
authors: Francesco Crescenzo Grasso; Pietro Liguori; Roberto Natella; Domenico Cotroneo

title: ABench: Adversarily Benchmarking Large Language Models across Taxonomized Values
abstract: Ensuring the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with diverse cultural values is critical for their safe global deployment. However, existing alignment benchmarks are predominantly English-centric or confined to simple discriminative tasks. Moreover, they often fail to effectively evaluate model robustness against complex, adversarial inductions within specific cultural contexts. To address these limitations, we propose ABench, a fine-grained, handcrafted benchmark specifically tailored to taxonomized values in Chinese. Grounded in a rigorous hierarchical taxonomy comprising 158 derived value subcategories, ABench consists of 2,895 open-ended questions. These questions employ techniques such as role-playing and logical traps to probe the stability of models' stances in adversarially induced contexts. Furthermore, we propose a weighted automated evaluation framework that utilizes question-specific scoring criteria for nuanced assessment. Extensive experiments on 16 mainstream LLMs reveal that most models exhibit significant vulnerabilities when subjected to sophisticated adversary attacks on values (scoring below 60). This underscores the need for more robust, culturally specific alignment strategies. Our data will be publicly released to promote further research on taxonomized value alignment.
authors: Liping Yang; Yongqi Leng; Jingting Zheng; Yuqi Ren; Shaolin Zhu; Deyi Xiong

title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.
authors: Navyansh Mahla; Sashank Vandrangi

title: SymLift: Neural Semantic Lifting for Compile-Free Vulnerability Detection in Context-Incomplete Code Fragments
abstract: Missing project context can prevent build-dependent analyzers from constructing program relations required for vulnerability detection, while neural predictions alone do not establish auditable derivations. We present SymLift, a compile-free framework centered on Vulnerability-Oriented Neural Semantic Lifting for context-incomplete code fragments. A fine-tuned large language model reconstructs vulnerability-relevant control-flow, data-flow, memory, and resource relations in a constrained LLVM-like intermediate representation (IR), without reconstructing the full project context or directly predicting vulnerability labels. A deterministic parser validates the IR and maps its supported operations and relations into normalized evidence facts. Explicit Datalog rules derive findings with supporting facts and derivation traces, ensuring deterministic reasoning for fixed facts and rules. We evaluate SymLift on FormAI, Juliet, and MegaVul. Reducing complete Juliet programs to function-level fragments lowers Clang compilation success from 100% to 12.00%, whereas SymLift's analysis completion rate decreases by only 1.17 percentage points. After task-specific fine-tuning, the lifter achieves a control-flow intersection over union (IoU) of 96.85% on FormAI. SymLift-Qwen-7B achieves a Target-F1 of 94.41% on FormAI and, across six vulnerability families on MegaVul, a micro-averaged precision of 98.24% and a micro-averaged Target-F1 of 91.66%. These results support accurate and auditable detection in the evaluated context-incomplete settings, even with partial program relations.
authors: Xiarun Chen; Jiaxing Xu; Bozhi Wu; Chenhui Cui; Chunrong Fang; Weiping Wen; Tao Li; Rubing Huang; Tsong Yueh Chen

title: CVE-to-ATT&CK Mapping via Evidence-Constrained Ranking
abstract: Mapping CVEs to MITRE ATT&CK techniques helps defenders translate vulnerability information into hypotheses about adversary behavior. Automating this mapping is challenging because relevant evidence is fragmented across heterogeneous security sources. In addition, ATT&CK techniques can be semantically similar, and existing annotations cover a highly long-tailed subset of the technique space. Existing supervised, retrieval-based, and LLM-based approaches therefore face limitations from closed-set supervision, semantic ambiguity, or unconstrained prediction. We formulate CVE-to-ATT&CK mapping as multi-evidence constrained ranking. Our framework TRACE first integrates complementary structural and semantic evidence from multiple sources to construct a bounded, high-coverage candidate pool over the complete ATT&CK technique space. It then reranks the retained candidates by combining their accumulated evidence with CVE--technique textual interactions and frequency-aware scoring. We evaluate the framework across six public datasets with different annotation processes and vulnerability distributions. Candidate construction reduces the 201-technique ATT&CK search space by approximately 60% while retaining at least one ground-truth technique for 95.11%-100% of CVEs. These results show that combining heterogeneous security evidence with constrained ranking provides a more controlled and generalizable bridge from vulnerability information to adversary behavior.
authors: Kai Wei; Yuwen Cui; Kehan Shen; Guangjing Wang

title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.
